lead: Blood pressure is the pressure of blood inside an artery, quoted as two numbers: systolic, the peak during a heartbeat, and diastolic, the trough between beats. Their difference is the pulse pressure, and the mean arterial pressure (MAP) is the average that pushes blood to the organs. These numbers detect hypertension, guide treatment in shock or on a ventilator, and check that a drug is working. The same pressure can be read by a sensor placed inside the artery (direct) or by a cuff wrapped round the arm (indirect).
prereq: You need: physiological transducers, the strain-gauge bridge and bio-amplifiers (see Physiological transducers and load cells, and Bio-amplifiers and data acquisition systems).

sections.h3: Direct measurement: sensor inside the artery

blocks.text: A cannula is inserted into the radial artery at the wrist, sometimes the brachial or femoral artery. It connects to a stiff saline-filled catheter that ends at a strain-gauge transducer. The transducer has a diaphragm with a strain gauge bridge bonded to it: pressure bends the diaphragm, the bridge changes resistance, a bridge amplifier converts that to a voltage, and a monitor draws the pulse waveform. This is the reference method. It gives a beat-by-beat waveform, not just two numbers, so it is used in intensive care and during surgery.

items: Flush the catheter with saline and remove all bubbles.
Zero the transducer at the level of the right atrium, roughly the mid-axillary line, with the tap open to air.
Turn the tap to the artery and check the waveform on the monitor.
Read systolic and diastolic from the waveform; in a ventilated patient read at end-expiration.

blocks.text: The catheter and transducer form a second-order system with a natural frequency and a damping ratio. If the damping ratio is too low, the trace rings or overshoots after each systolic peak, and systolic pressure reads falsely high. If the natural frequency is too low, the trace cannot follow the fast systolic upstroke, the peaks are blunted and systolic pressure reads low. A bubble in the line adds compliance, lowers the natural frequency and flattens the trace, so the systolic peak is lost.

blocks.where: MAP is mean arterial pressure in mmHg; S is systolic pressure in mmHg; D is diastolic pressure in mmHg. The formula holds at normal heart rates.

blocks.text: An inflatable rubber bladder inside a cloth cuff is wrapped round the upper arm and pumped above systolic pressure. The brachial artery is squeezed shut and flow stops. Air is let out slowly. When cuff pressure falls just below systolic, blood squirts through the partly open artery as a turbulent jet, the artery wall vibrates, and a stethoscope over the artery below the cuff hears the sound. These are Korotkoff sounds, named after Nikolai Korotkov, the Russian surgeon who described them in 1905.

Phase V is diastolic in most adults. In some patients the sounds never disappear: children, pregnancy and aortic regurgitation are common reasons. If sounds are still heard when the cuff pressure reaches zero, phase IV (muffling) is taken as diastolic instead.

The mercury manometer is a vertical glass tube; cuff pressure pushes mercury up a calibrated scale. It is accurate but is being withdrawn because mercury is toxic. The aneroid manometer uses a Bourdon tube or bellows moving a needle, and it needs regular calibration. In the palpatory method the operator feels the radial pulse return as the cuff falls; this gives systolic pressure only, and it is used when sounds are hard to hear. A Doppler probe over the artery detects the frequency shift from moving blood and is used in infants and in peripheral arteries.

sections.h3: Oscillometric method and sources of error

blocks.text: Automated oscillometric monitors use the same cuff but no microphone. A pressure sensor watches the small pressure pulses that the artery pushes into the cuff as it opens and closes with each beat. The size of these oscillations rises to a maximum and then falls. The cuff pressure at maximum oscillation is taken as MAP; the machine then finds systolic and diastolic from fixed ratios of the oscillation amplitude, for example systolic where the amplitude has risen to about half of its maximum and diastolic where it has fallen to about 0.8 of it. Each maker uses its own ratios, tested against the auscultatory method. The method needs no trained ear, works through thin clothing, and is used in home monitors and ward machines.

items: Cuff too narrow: reads falsely high. The bladder should be about 40 percent of the arm circumference in width and about 80 percent of the arm circumference in length, so that it wraps most of the way round the arm.
Arm below heart level: reads high, roughly 0.8 mmHg for every centimetre of drop.
Deflation faster than 3 mmHg per second: underestimates systolic and overestimates diastolic.
Talking, a full bladder, caffeine or anxiety all raise the reading. A rise seen only in the clinic, with normal home readings, is the white-coat effect.

spec.aria: Cuff pressure falling from 160 mmHg at 3 mmHg per second against time, with Korotkoff sounds from 128 to 82 mmHg drawn as one tick per beat and phases I to V marked.

examples.question: A 12 cm wide cuff on an arm of 28 cm circumference is inflated to 160 mmHg and let down at 3 mmHg/s. Korotkoff sounds appear at 128 mmHg, become muffled at 100 mmHg and disappear at 82 mmHg. (a) Is the cuff the right size? (b) Give systolic, diastolic, pulse and mean arterial pressure, and systolic pressure in kPa (1 mmHg = 0.1333 kPa). (c) How long after deflation starts is the first sound heard? (d) A radial artery catheter in the same patient reads 134/80 mmHg. Why is it different, and does the mean pressure change?
steps: (a) Bladder width ÷ arm circumference = 12 ÷ 28 = 0.43, close to the 40 % rule, so the cuff is the right size.
(b) Systolic is the cuff pressure at the first Korotkoff sound: S = 128 mmHg. Diastolic is taken at phase V, where the sounds disappear: D = 82 mmHg. Phase IV at 100 mmHg is noted, not used.
Pulse pressure = S − D = 128 − 82 = 46 mmHg. MAP = D + (S − D)/3 = 82 + 46/3 = 82 + 15.3 = 97.3 mmHg.
(c) The cuff falls from 160 to 128 mmHg, a drop of 32 mmHg, at 3 mmHg/s: 32 ÷ 3 = 10.7 s. It reaches 82 mmHg after 78 ÷ 3 = 26 s, so the whole reading takes about half a minute.

(d) Radial catheter MAP = 80 + (134 − 80)/3 = 80 + 18 = 98 mmHg, within 1 mmHg of the cuff value. As the pulse wave travels from the aorta to the wrist, reflected waves make the peak taller and the trough slightly lower (peripheral amplification). So the radial line reads systolic higher and diastolic a little lower than a cuff on the upper arm, while the mean pressure stays almost the same.
examples.answer: The cuff is the right size (0.43 of the arm). Systolic 128 mmHg (17.1 kPa), diastolic 82 mmHg, pulse pressure 46 mmHg, MAP 97.3 mmHg; the first sound comes 10.7 s after deflation starts. The radial line differs because of peripheral amplification, but its MAP of 98 mmHg matches the cuff.

traps: Writing phase IV (muffling, 100 mmHg) as diastolic when the examiner expects phase V (disappearance, 82 mmHg).
Forgetting that a cuff that is too narrow reads falsely high, and one that is too wide reads falsely low.
Zeroing the transducer at the shelf level instead of at the right atrium, which adds a hydrostatic error.
Mixing units: 1 mmHg = 0.1333 kPa, so a pressure in kPa is about 7.5 times smaller than the same pressure in mmHg.
Assuming an oscillometric machine finds systolic at the first oscillation; it takes the cuff pressure at maximum oscillation as MAP.

quiz.q: Define pulse pressure and give the formula for mean arterial pressure.
quiz.a: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic pressure. MAP = D + (S − D)/3, where S is systolic and D is diastolic pressure in mmHg.

quiz.q: Which Korotkoff phase is taken as diastolic pressure in the standard method?
quiz.a: Phase V, the point where the sound disappears.

quiz.q: Why does a bubble in the catheter line flatten the pressure trace?
quiz.a: A bubble is compressible, so it adds compliance to the fluid column. This lowers the natural frequency of the catheter–transducer system and damps the trace, so the sharp systolic peak is rounded off and reads lower.

quiz.q: Why does a cuff that is too narrow give a falsely high systolic reading?
quiz.a: A narrow bladder cannot compress the whole artery uniformly; the pressure must be raised higher before the artery closes, so both systolic and diastolic readings come out high.

quiz.q: A patient's cuff reading is 150/90 mmHg. Find the pulse pressure and the mean arterial pressure.
Why does an oscillometric monitor give MAP directly while the auscultatory method gives systolic and diastolic directly?
quiz.a: The oscillation amplitude is largest when the cuff pressure equals MAP, so the machine reads MAP from that peak. Systolic and diastolic are then computed from fixed amplitude ratios. The auscultatory method marks the onset and disappearance of sounds, which correspond to systolic and diastolic, so MAP must be calculated from them.

quiz.q: A patient with an irregular heart rhythm shows readings that vary by 10 mmHg between attempts. Give two reasons and one way to improve the reading.
quiz.a: Beat-to-beat stroke volume changes, so systolic pressure genuinely differs from beat to beat, and the deflation rate may skip the true first and last sounds. Take several readings, average them, and use a slower deflation rate or an oscillometric monitor that averages beats.

beyond: Not for the exam. Ward monitors combine an oscillometric cuff with an arterial-line input and reject readings taken at the wrong deflation rate. Research is moving to cuffless methods, such as a wrist device using pulse transit time, calibrated against a cuff. Search for "pulse transit time blood pressure" and "ISO 81060-2 validation".
